steps.name: Light the rim of the coat

lines.text: Let the meadow grass and the shaggy coat dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
Inside the outlined area. Its bottom is about 3 in from the bottom edge, and its left side is about 2 in from the left edge; it's about 7 in wide and 8 in tall.
The outline also reaches onto the highland cow and the cow's shaggy coat, painted already: there, only soften this paint into their edge and leave them showing.
Press the full width of the brush where the lock starts, then turn onto its edge and lighten the pressure as you pull outward along the lock.
It should leave hairs that start wide and taper to a point.
Pale gold is much lighter than what it goes over: expect two or three thin coats, letting each dry.

steps.meant: The cow's head, fringe and right side glow with a bright gold rim, much smaller than the locks under it. The horns have no light along their tops yet, and the cow has no nose.

steps.name: Light the tops of the horns

lines.text: Let the sunlit rim and the shaggy coat dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
Inside the outlined area. Its top is about 5 in from the top edge, and its left side is about 5 in from the left edge; it's about 1/4 in wide and 1/4 in tall.
The outline also reaches onto the horns' dark tips and the cow's horns, painted already: there, only soften this paint into their edge and leave them showing.
Bend every stroke with the horn: start near the head and follow the top of its curve out toward the tip.
It should leave marks that bend with the horn, which is what makes it look round.
Cream gold is much lighter than what it goes over: expect two or three thin coats, letting each dry.
Step back, squint, or take a photo to see it whole, and compare the big shapes with the picture.

steps.meant: The horns have a pale cream light along their tops over the tan, with the dark tips and undersides still showing. The cow has no nose yet.
